strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a timely and under-explored failure mode, multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing, and distinguishes it from single-agent visual hallucination by emphasizing inter-agent textual propagation.

It provides an extensive empirical analysis across turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention, showing reduced visual attention allocation over agent turns and identifying middle-layer unimodal vision tokens as potentially important for visual information relay.

The proposed ViF method is simple and broadly applicable: it relays selected visual tokens and applies attention reallocation, and it is evaluated across 8 benchmarks, 4 MAS structures, and 10 base VLMs, with consistent average improvements and substantial reductions in the proposed hallucination snowballing score.

The paper includes a useful set of comparisons against five existing hallucination mitigation methods, ablations on relay tokens and attention reallocation, hyperparameter analyses, an alternative Key-Norm selection strategy, and broader cross-model results in the appendix.
The scope of the experimental effort is strong, especially the combination of multiple MAS structures, model families, model scales, and both comprehensive and hallucination-focused benchmarks.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not fully established: the paper shows correlation between reduced visual attention and hallucination snowballing, but does not rigorously identify attention reduction as the cause rather than a symptom or side effect of longer multi-turn textual context.

The token-selection analysis may overstate the uniqueness of unimodal vision tokens: in the main ablation, rise and fall token subsets produce similar performance drops to unimodal tokens in the middle layers, so the evidence that unimodal tokens are specially critical is weaker than claimed.

Method clarity and reproducibility are limited: it is unclear exactly how relay tokens are selected at each turn, how contextualization handles changing instructions/questions across turns, whether the added transformer block requires per-model training, and how plug-and-play the method is in practice without code.

The newly proposed HS metric is not validated against human judgments or existing metrics, and its weighting formula and use of a judge model make the large reported HS reductions difficult to interpret; comparisons against single-agent hallucination methods using this metric may also be unfair or overstate the benefit.

Original-metric improvements are modest on average (roughly 2-4%), lack variance/statistical significance tests, and sometimes include regressions such as CHAIR worsening in a few settings, so the practical significance of the gains is not fully guaranteed.
There is no efficiency, latency, or memory analysis despite the extra trainable module, token selection, and attention modification, which is important for multi-agent deployments.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, such as the statement that dropping unimodal tokens degrades performance 'almost three times' more than other subsets, which is not supported by the reported table where rise/fall subsets are comparable.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: hallucination propagation in multi-agent VLM systems.
Provides turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention analyses, which could be informative if validated and properly controlled.
Evaluates across multiple benchmarks, MAS structures, and base models, showing effort toward generality.
The idea of relaying visual evidence via selected visual tokens rather than pure textual messages is intuitive and potentially useful.
weaknesses: Fundamental experimental confound: the method trains/fine-tunes the base VLM (Appendix Table 8 shows the LLM is trainable in Stage Two), while the baselines are off-the-shelf, untrained models. Improvements may therefore come from instruction tuning rather than the proposed ViF. No training-only baseline is provided.
Contradicts the 'plug-and-play' and 'lightweight' claims: the approach requires training a transformer block and fine-tuning the LLM, so it is not a purely plug-and-play inference-time method.

Missing critical baselines: no comparison to simply passing the original image or raw visual tokens to every agent, nor to prior MAS-specific hallucination-propagation methods (e.g., Zhong et al., 2024).

Evaluation is weakened by an unvalidated, ad hoc HS metric. The definitions of hallucination severity h_i and propagation distance d_i are unclear, yet HS is used as key evidence for large improvements.
Inconsistent experimental results: main Table 1 numbers do not match Appendix Table 12 (e.g., random middle-layer drops are 38.4 vs. 78.9), raising serious concerns about reliability or reporting.

Attention analysis is confounded: attention allocation is aggregated by token type while token counts change across turns. The apparent reduction in vision attention may simply reflect an increasing number of text tokens rather than over-reliance on text.
Method details are insufficient for reproducibility: unimodal token selection, buffer-token strategy, reallocation equations, and training data are not fully specified; code is not available.
The attention-reallocation equations are mathematically unclear and may break normalization; it is not isolated whether reallocation is applied during training or only at inference.
Reported gains are small (often 1–3 points) and lack variance, significance tests, or per-category analysis; some results do not improve or even worsen (e.g., CHAIR).
Claims of consistent improvement across all benchmarks/models/structures are overstated; larger models are only tested on the circular structure, not across all four MAS structures.
Writing and presentation quality are poor: wrong table references (e.g., citing Table 6 for HS results), inconsistent notation, grammatical errors, and reference mistakes.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a novel and practically relevant failure mode, multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing, clearly distinguishing intrinsic hallucination from inter-agent propagation.

Provides systematic turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention analyses and an ablation over vision-token subsets, yielding a plausible mechanism: declining visual attention and diminishing unimodal middle-layer vision tokens.
Proposes a coherent mitigation paradigm, ViF, combining visual relay tokens and attention reallocation, with a practical Key-Norm alternative for Flash-Attention models.
Evaluation is broad: eight benchmarks, four MAS structures, ten base VLMs up to 34B parameters, plus comparisons against five single-model hallucination-mitigation methods and several ablations.
Reports consistent improvements across many settings, especially on hallucination-oriented benchmarks and larger models, and provides hyperparameter analyses and an HS metric to quantify snowballing.
weaknesses: The “plug-and-play/lightweight” claim conflicts with the training pipeline: Table 8 indicates the LLM is trainable in stage two and the added transformer block is trained, so the method is not obviously plug-and-play or training-free relative to off-the-shelf baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete: training data, training data construction, and exact judge/evaluation details for the HS metric are not specified, and the source code is only promised rather than released.

The proposed HS metric is author-designed and its operational definition is underspecified; the large reported HS reductions may partly reflect metric design, while improvements on original metrics are often modest (e.g., 1–3 points).

Causality is not fully established: the link between reduced visual attention and hallucination snowballing is primarily correlational, and alternative explanations such as long-context attention dilution or textual-context growth are not sufficiently ruled out.

The comparison to single-model hallucination-mitigation methods is informative but somewhat unequal, since those methods are not designed for MAS; stronger MAS-specific baselines or uncontrolled-training comparisons would help.

The method depends on attention/Key-Norm token selection and several hyperparameters, and the selected unimodal token proportion becomes extremely small in later turns, raising robustness concerns; there are also minor table issues (e.g., AMBER direction in Table 4).

strengths: Introduces and formalizes a novel and practically relevant problem: multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing, distinct from single-agent hallucination or prior textual snowballing work.

Provides systematic turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention analyses to diagnose visual attention degradation and identify middle-layer unimodal vision tokens as important for relaying visual evidence.

Proposes ViF, a conceptually simple and model-agnostic mitigation method based on visual relay tokens and attention reallocation, with an alternative attention-score-free selection strategy for Flash-Attention models.

The empirical evaluation is broad: four MAS structures, ten base VLMs including 30B+ models, eight main benchmarks plus augmented multi-image/video benchmarks, ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, efficiency, adversarial correction, and case studies.
Reports consistent improvements in multi-agent settings and provides code, latency/FLOPs analyses, and extensive appendix experiments.
weaknesses: The main-text Table 1 is badly inconsistent: many entries are non-monotonic and contradict the appendix (e.g., Random/Inactive/Rise/Fall results often drop to implausible values such as 6.6 at 50% deep dropping), which directly undermines the central token-importance analysis and stated ratios in the main paper.

Table 4 reports an Avg column that is numerically incompatible with the listed benchmark scores (e.g., 33.9, 42.3, 44.3, 52.0 followed by Avg 72.8), raising serious concerns about evaluation reporting and table correctness.

The method section omits key training details: the loss and supervision for the transformer block f, training data for visual relay token contextualization, and how attention reallocation is optimized or tuned. Reproducibility relies heavily on the appendix but is still not fully clear from the main text.

The proposed Hallucination Snowballing (HS) metric relies on GPT-5 as a judge and lacks strong human or multi-judge validation beyond a limited Gemini agreement check on POPE. Since many headline gains are on HS rather than standard metrics, the reliability of the main improvement claims is uncertain.
The arrows and metric directions for HS are sometimes inconsistent (e.g., AMBER marked with ↑ in Table 5 while lower HS is better), making the evaluation harder to interpret.

The comparison to single-agent hallucination mitigation methods adapted to MAS may be somewhat unfair because those methods are not designed for multi-agent propagation; a more careful discussion of adaptation and hyperparameter tuning for each baseline is needed.

Gains on standard comprehensive benchmarks are modest (often 2-4%), while much larger gains are claimed via the newly introduced HS metric. The paper would be stronger with more rigorous validation of HS and clearer separation between standard benchmark performance and HS-based conclusions.
The scope is limited to decentralized MAS structures; centralized MAS, other collaboration protocols, and broader model families are not explored, though the paper acknowledges some limitations.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and relevant failure mode: multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing in VLM-based multi-agent systems, and links it to reduced attention to vision tokens across agent turns.

The turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention analyses, while not fully conclusive, provide useful qualitative evidence that later agents increasingly attend to instruction/text tokens rather than visual evidence.

The proposed ViF combines visual relay tokens with attention reallocation, and the paper evaluates it across many benchmarks, four MAS structures, and up to ten base VLMs, showing broad empirical coverage.
The ablation and sensitivity analyses are relatively comprehensive, covering relay-token count, attention reallocation, hyperparameters, efficiency, and adversarial/noisy settings.
The method is relatively lightweight in terms of reported latency and FLOPs overhead, which is a practical strength if the reported efficiency numbers are accurate.
Case studies illustrate how visual flow may prevent early errors from being propagated in a few qualitative examples.
weaknesses: Major evaluation inconsistency: Table 4 reports augmented visual benchmarks where ViF often degrades performance relative to baselines (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT-7B on MuirBench 42.6→42.3, MVBench 49.2→44.3, Video-MME 60.4→52.0; similar regressions for other models), yet the text claims consistent improvement. Worse, the Avg. values in Table 4 (e.g., 72.8, 72.2, 72.5, 74.0) do not match the average of the four listed metrics, strongly undermining confidence in the reported results.

The central causal claim that reduced visual attention causes hallucination snowballing is not convincingly established. The evidence is largely correlational, and the token-dropping analyses do not isolate attention allocation from other confounding factors.

The claim that unimodal vision tokens are uniquely critical is overstated. In Table 1, unimodal-token ablation is not consistently three times worse than rise/fall subsets, especially in middle layers where the differences are much smaller than the text suggests.

The new HS metric is not validated. It relies on an LLM judge (GPT-5) and a custom scoring function, and there is no demonstration that the metric measures hallucination propagation rather than artifacts of the judge or the scoring design. This weakens the main claims about 30–40% snowballing reduction.

Comparisons in Table 6 may be unfair. Single-model hallucination mitigation methods (MemVR, VISTA, FarSight, DeCo, TAME) are applied in a multi-agent context without clear adaptation or tuning, so their apparent failure in MAS is not strong evidence that ViF is superior for MAS.

Main benchmark improvements are modest and lack statistical support. Many gains are 1–3 absolute points with no error bars, significance tests, or variance across seeds/runs, so claims like “markedly reduces hallucination snowballing” are not sufficiently supported.

Novelty and technical depth are limited. The core idea—relaying selected visual tokens between agents and reallocating attention—is an incremental combination of existing attention-based visual token selection and inference-time attention modification ideas. The additional transformer block used for contextualizing relay tokens also raises questions about whether the method is truly training-free or model-agnostic.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The source code link in the abstract is blank, training details are incomplete, and key choices such as how the transformer block is trained per base model, how many training examples are used, and whether hyperparameters were tuned on test benchmarks are not sufficiently specified.

The attention reallocation equations and masks are not fully explained, and it is unclear whether the intervention preserves the pretrained model’s behavior or introduces systematic distortion. The hyperparameter choices appear tuned directly on the evaluation benchmarks without an independent validation split.

The paper uses a non-trivial, potentially fragile token-selection rule based on attention “unimodal” peaks. For FlashAttention models, the alternative Key-Norm strategy is heuristic and depends on buffer tokens, making the method less principled and harder to reproduce.

Several tables and figures are confusingly presented: Table 5 lacks clear labels for baseline vs. +Ours rows; Table 4’s Avg. column is unexplained; and the text sometimes claims improvements that are inconsistent with the displayed numbers.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a novel and practically important failure mode, multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing, and distinguishes it from prior single-agent hallucination work.
Provides systematic turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention analyses that link visual attention degradation and diminishing unimodal vision tokens to hallucination propagation in MAS.

Proposes a clear and intuitive mitigation method, ViF, combining visual relay tokens with attention reallocation; the Key-Norm alternative makes the approach compatible with Flash-Attention-based models.

Evaluation is extensive: eight main benchmarks, four MAS structures, ten base VLMs from 7B to 34B, additional augmented visual benchmarks, ablations, sensitivity analyses, efficiency measurements, adversarial robustness, and comparisons with multiple single-agent hallucination mitigation methods.
Demonstrates substantial reductions in the proposed hallucination snowballing score and consistent main-benchmark improvements, with code and detailed appendix materials provided for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Some tables in the provided manuscript appear internally inconsistent or ambiguous, especially Table 4, where individual augmented-benchmark metrics show degradation while the reported average is not interpretable as an average of those metrics; Table 1 also has non-monotonic dropping results that complicate interpretation.
No statistical significance tests or multiple-run variance are reported, so the robustness of the frequently modest (2–4%) improvements is unclear.

The comparison with single-agent hallucination mitigation methods may be somewhat unfavorable, since those methods were not designed for multi-agent settings and are applied without adaptation; integration details could materially affect the conclusions.

The method assumes access to internal attention or hidden states and trains an additional transformer block per base VLM, limiting applicability to API-only/closed-source MAS and raising unaddressed practicality/privacy considerations.

The proposed HS metric depends on a GPT-5 judge and is not validated against human judgments; although robustness is briefly checked, the metric's sensitivity and construct validity remain underexplored.
The abstract omits the actual source-code URL, and several implementation details—especially token selection in later turns and compatibility when agents use different models—are not fully specified.
